text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- Chamber of Economy raises new demands in pension debate including that women with no children should be allowed to retire later but the government does not want to bring in equal retirement ages for men and women until the year 2,019.
- Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel came under fire from parliament over allegations he called Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer a "real pig".
- The dollar and pound extended a gains against the schilling partly due to the fact that there was no U.S. interest rate rise.
- The deputy head of Creditanstalt Max Kothbauer was appointed as head of postal savings bank P.S.K.
- Austrian lawyers say a new government drive permitting the bugging of lawyers, journalists, clergy and doctors, is an infringement of basic rights.
- From September 41 shares from eastern European markets will be traded on the electronic Equos trading system of the Vienna bourse.
- The justice ministry has drafted a new takeover law to protect small shareholders.
- The govenrment has agreed to introduce a new telecoms law by August 1, which will form the basis for the EU-proscribed liberalisation of the telecoms market at the start of 1998.

- Austria will easily make the hurdles to a single currency. The International Monetary Fund estimates that Austria's budget deficit will be 2.5 percent in 1997. The finance ministry confirmed that revenues in the first half were 20.3 billion schillings above the year before.
- Schuessel will not take legal action against allegations he lied about his comments on Tietmeyer. Market researchers say the incident has done his image irreparable damage.
- Whether or not pension reforms go through depends on the civil servants, a study by German expert Bert Ruerup said.
- Tourists are avoiding shopping in Austria. Austria lacks enticing buys and unique offers, a researcher says.
